The three days are dated four different ways. Gill counts by the Jewish calendar: Moses died on the seventh of Adar, the thirty days of mourning ended on the seventh of Nisan, the spies were sent two days before that and returned on the eighth, so the morning Joshua rose early was the ninth, the crossing falling on the tenth. Clarke takes them as the spies' own errand, so they returned on the third day and the proclamation followed at once; and he adds a dating from Usher, the twenty-eighth of April in the fortieth year after the exodus, with the distance from Shittim to Jordan given from Josephus as about eight English miles. Calvin reckons from the announcement rather than the departure, three days after it was intimated, since they did not halt at the bank longer than one night. Henry is interested not in the arithmetic but in the marching: they went forward in faith though not yet told how they should pass, and we must go on in the way of duty though we foresee difficulties, depending on divine sufficiency for what we are not sufficient for. He makes the early rising a character note: those that would bring great things to pass must rise early.

Whether the pillar was still with them divides two of them flatly. Henry infers that the pillar of cloud and fire was removed, since otherwise it would have led them, though he allows that it may now have hovered over the ark, giving them a double guide. Wesley takes that alternative as the likelier: till this time the ark went in the middle of the cloudy pillar and now goes in front, the pillar probably still hovering over it. On the two thousand cubits Clarke gives two plain reasons: the greater respect due to the symbol of the divine presence, and that the ark which was to pilot them might be the more conspicuous, which it could not be had the people crowded upon it. Calvin agrees the interval declares the ark's dignity, recalling what happened to Uzzah when with inconsiderate zeal he put forth his hand to support it; but he adds a reason nobody else reaches, that the distance exercised their faith by keeping them from confining God's grace within narrow limits, and reminded them that though far from the ark his power was ever near. Gill notices the marginal reading between you and them, and disposes of what grew out of it — a Jewish fiction of two arks travelling together, that of the divine Majesty and that holding Joseph's bones, which three rabbis notice but which has no foundation in the text.

The last two verses raise two smaller questions. On sanctifying themselves, Clarke supposes the command implied what Moses had required before, that they wash themselves and their garments and abstain from whatever might indispose their minds; Wesley asks it of soul and body both. Calvin declines to settle it, the Hebrew word bearing more than one sense and either suiting, so he thought it best to leave a free choice; but he rejects one reading as too confined, that the people were to purge themselves merely so nothing might impede the passage. On the priests carrying the ark, Clarke calls it remarkable that this fell to them and not the Levites whose ordinary business it was, and reports a conjecture that the ark was carried uncovered here, not wrapped in its curtains as the Levites carried it. Wesley states the rule more simply: although the Levites were to carry the ark, the priests might perform that office and did so on some solemn occasions. Keil supplies structure rather than detail, noting that Joshua's issuing these commands with a prediction of the miracle presupposes that the Lord had already made his will known to him.
7:
Henry reads the passage as an exchange of honours: God magnifies Joshua so the people may magnify him, and Joshua turns it back by making them know whose God it is. He notes that God spoke to Joshua as he had to Moses from off the mercy-seat, which would make him easy in himself and great among the people; and he draws the parallel the passage invites, that as the dividing of the Red Sea convinced Israel God was with Moses in bringing them out, so the dividing of Jordan convinces them he is with Joshua in bringing them in. He adds a coincidence nobody else notices, that God began to magnify Joshua at the banks of Jordan and at the same place began to magnify our Lord as Mediator, John having baptized at Bethabara, the house of passage.

Why the crossing had to be miraculous is Henry's question, and his answer turns on what would not have served. God could by a sudden frost have congealed the surface, so that they might all have gone over upon the ice; but that being a thing sometimes done in that country by the ordinary power of nature, it would not have been such an honour to Israel's God nor such a terror to Israel's enemies. It had therefore to be done in a way with no precedent but the dividing of the Red Sea, that miracle being repeated to show God has the same power to finish the salvation of his people that he had to begin it. He finds a second purpose in its form: by dividing the waters and making the dry land appear, God reminded them of what Moses had taught of the work of creation, so what they saw might assist their belief of what they read, and they might know the God they worshipped was the same that made the world.

How far the sign reaches is Calvin's question, and he makes it a matter of prudence. The power of the miracle extends further than the entrance of the land, since merely to open a passage into hostile territory with no retreat would have been exposure to death, the people destroyed among straits in an unknown region or worn out by want. When God restores the river to its course it is as if he stretched forth his hand to rout the inhabitants, so the passage is a presage of the victory to come; and let us learn prudently to combine the acts of divine goodness relating to our salvation, so that a happy commencement keeps alive the hope of an equally happy end. But he will not let the miracle stand as the ground of faith. When Joshua says the people will know God's presence from it, he indirectly upbraids them with their distrust, since the mere promise ought to have sufficed; though experimental knowledge may still act as a secondary support to faith's weakness, for what God promises in word he seals by act. Clarke reads the same verse as assurance for men apt to faint at danger, contrasting the living God with idolaters who have only gods of wood and stone; and he sets out where each of the seven nations lay — the Canaanites about Tyre and Sidon, the Hittites in the mountains southward, the Hivites by Ebal and Gerizim, the Girgashites beyond Jordan, the Jebusites in Jerusalem, the Amorites near the Dead Sea, and the Perizzites probably no distinct nation at all but villagers scattered through the country. On the title given to God the grammarians divide. Gill reports that some Jewish and Christian interpreters, on the strength of an accent distinguishing the word covenant, read it as calling the ark itself the Lord of all the earth; Keil rejects that construction by name as a mistaken exposition, holding the genitive to depend on covenant.
14:
Henry and Clarke answer the same objection, and both answer it from the season. Clarke reports the remark often made, that no miracle was needed since the Jordan is an inconsiderable stream easily fordable and but twenty yards across; and replies that the historian's aside proves there was a season when the river overflowed its banks. The Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon, covered with snow through the winter months, so the river is low then; but when the summer sun has melted the snows there is a prodigious increase of waters the old channel cannot contain. God chose that time, he concludes, precisely so a miraculous interposition might be necessary. Henry makes it an argument about Providence: the flood coming just then, when it might have been restrained or the crossing ordered at another season, very much magnified the power of God — for though the opposition given to the salvation of God's people have all imaginable advantages, it is as easy to Omnipotence to divide a river filled to the brim as one ever so narrow.

How far the water had spread is disputed within Calvin's own pages. He takes the plain to have been covered, so the line of the banks and the ford could not be observed and the slime spread far and wide, increasing the priests' fear; and he praises their valour, since they might have expected on putting in their feet to find a deep pool and be engulfed, yet moved firmly forward to the appointed place. A note printed with his text disputes the premise: the clause does not bear the meaning he and the English translators assigned it, since his rendering has the Jordan full beyond all his banks where the original says only that it fills them completely, the Greek version and Luther's agreeing. The difference is slight, the note allows, but of importance, because such differences have furnished the infidel with plausible grounds for assailing the credit of the narrative — it having been insinuated that the historian exaggerated the inundation in order to heighten the miracle.

On what the miracle consisted in Calvin is more precise than the others, and concedes something first. It is not impossible, he grants, that the flowing might have been restrained for a short time so that some portion of the channel appeared dry, or that the course might have changed; but it was certainly neither a natural nor a fortuitous event when the waters stood gathered up into a heap. He turns that heap into an image of what they walked through: what stood beside them was a grave in which the whole multitude would have been buried had the waters resumed their liquid state, so that they were saved in the midst of death. Henry notices a difference pointing the same way — at the Red Sea the waters were a wall on either hand, here only on the right — and observes that the God of nature can turn fluids into solids, and that he sometimes cleaves the earth with rivers and sometimes, as here, cleaves the rivers without earth. He gives three reasons for crossing over against Jericho: a bold defiance of one of the strongest cities, encouragement to themselves with so pleasant a country in view, and terror to enemies who were amazed spectators. On the priests standing still, Henry finds two purposes: to try their faith by giving them their post with mountains of water over their heads, and to encourage the people, who might go through fearing no evil in what was for the moment a valley of the shadow of death. Keil confines himself to the words: they stood in the bed of the river, not merely by it, and with a firm foot. Gill is exact about where they began: not at the bank, which was overflowed, but at the water's edge.
